title: Google AI Co-Scientist Generates Wet-Lab-Validated Biomedical Discoveries
whyItMatters: Multi-agent Gemini co-scientist independently proposed novel liver-fibrosis epigenetic targets, AML drug candidates, and a bacterial gene-transfer mechanism—all validated in wet labs.
summary: Google Research, Stanford, and Imperial College London unveiled a multi-agent hypothesis-generation system powered by Gemini that uses tournament evolution and self-critique to propose testable research plans. In wet-lab validation, it identified drug repurposing candidates inhibiting acute myeloid leukemia, proposed epigenetic targets blocking scarring in human liver organoids, and independently reproduced in two days an unpublished antimicrobial-resistance gene-transfer mechanism that took Imperial researchers a decade to uncover.
technicalHighlights: Independently derived an unpublished capsid-forming phage-inducible chromosomal island (cf-PICI) transfer hypothesis matching 10 years of Imperial College bench work.
Proposed novel epigenetic targets for liver fibrosis validated with statistically significant anti-fibrotic activity in human hepatic organoids at Stanford.
Graduated from February 2025 preprint to a peer-reviewed Nature publication in May 2026 after testing across 100+ institutions.
caveats: Synthesizes existing scientific literature at superhuman breadth rather than performing physical bench experiments; human wet-lab teams remain essential for experimental validation.

scoreRationale.foundational: Validated multi-agent tournament hypothesis generation as a viable discovery engine in experimental biomedicine.
scoreRationale.ripple: Already integrated into Gemini for Science and tested across over 100 biomedical research institutions.
scoreRationale.verification: Wet-lab validated across three independent biomedical labs and published in Nature (May 2026).
scoreRationale.velocity: Recapitulated a decade-long antimicrobial resistance discovery in two days of multi-agent compute.
